title: The burning bush (Exodus 3:1–6)
hookLine: a bush burns and is not consumed, and Moses turns aside to look
tomorrow: a name that is a verb

cards: Moses has a quiet life now. He married Tzipporah, one of the young women he helped at the well. He has a son.
He keeps sheep for his father-in-law, Jethro. Years go by; the palace is a memory. One day he leads the flock deep into the wilderness, to a mountain called Horeb.
Ordinary work, an ordinary day. Out of the corner of his eye, he sees a bush on fire. In the desert, dry brush catches.
Plenty of people would keep walking.

teach.b: Here's what makes it strange: "the bush was not consumed." It's burning, and it doesn't burn up.

teach.h: I WILL TURN ASIDE NOW, AND SEE.
teach.b: Moses says: "I will turn aside now, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt."

teach.h: WHEN GOD SAW THAT HE TURNED ASIDE.
teach.b: Then the verse that makes the whole story: "And when the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called unto him out of the midst of the bush." Read it slowly. The call comes after Moses stops.
It's as if the fire was burning for anyone who'd notice, and Moses was the one who did. Some teachers have pointed out that you'd only know the bush wasn't burning up if you watched it for a while.
A glance wouldn't tell you. You'd have to stay. Then God calls: "Moses, Moses."
And he answers: "Here am I." Hineni, the same word Abraham said.

Then: don't come closer; "put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." Ordinary dirt, on a mountain where sheep had been grazing, and the text calls it holy ground.
Why a thorn bush, a lowly desert plant?
The midrash answers: to show that God is with the people in their suffering, in the thorns, not only in the cedars.

Some have read the bush that isn't destroyed as a picture of Israel itself, burning under slavery, and still there. Moses hides his face, afraid to look at God. He's about to find out why he was called.

how: Jewish tradition reads the burning bush as the moment Moses is called, and teachers often use it to talk about noticing holiness in ordinary places; the Hebrew word for bush, sneh, is heard as an echo of Sinai.

o: holy ground, the place where God appears
a thorn bush burning but never used up
here am I: answering a call, fully present

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: the mountain where Moses kept sheep

s: God called to Moses before he turned aside
"when the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called unto him."
the burning bush was a thorn bush
the Hebrew is sneh, a lowly desert thorn. the midrash says God is with the people in their suffering.
Moses looked straight at God in the bush
he hid his face, afraid to look.

games.q: you're a shepherd in the desert, far from anyone. out of the corner of your eye, a bush is on fire. what do you do?
o: run back to camp to warn people.
games.why: Moses turns aside to see why the bush isn't burning up. only then does God call his name.

practice: Find one ordinary thing right where you are: light on a wall, the grain of a table, your own hand, a plant, a sound outside.
Turn aside to it the way Moses did, and stay with it longer than you normally would, as you'd watch a fire that doesn't go out. What do you see now that you didn't see a minute ago?

wordCard.voice: Hineni, here am I, the word Moses answers with at the bush, the same word Abraham once said when God called him.

orig.note: Hebrew: a thorn bush. the rabbis heard in it an echo of Sinai, the mountain to come.

carryVoice: Your line: turn aside and see. Holy ground can look like ordinary dirt. That's day eighty-one.
